extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, naturalists, and the scientifically literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Experimental procedures and interpretive criteria for detecting and characterising 'abnormal' (reversed or non-solar-order) dispersion in solutions and small fragments of surface‑coloured bodies using liquid prisms, hollow prisms, and spectroscopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquid-prism observation method (Christiansen/Kundt)
rubrics_metrics.description: A drop of the concentrated solution is placed on a glass plate; over this drop a second glass plate (same breadth) is fixed at an angle of about 25° so that a very thin prismatic layer of liquid (scarcely broader than a hair) adjacent to the line of contact is produced and is transparent for most colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View a narrow bright flame or an illuminated slit through this thin layer; carry the liquid prism to the place of the glass prism in a Bunsen & Kirchhoff spectroscope; the most favourable angle for the liquid prism is determined by trial; observations require practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against reflection/refraction artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers must be on their guard against deception arising from phenomena of reflection or refraction when examining the thin liquid prism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful technique and experience are required to distinguish true anomalous dispersion from spurious effects produced by surface reflections or ordinary refraction; verify by changing geometry and concentrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hollow prism and immersion trough (Soret method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pour the solution into a hollow prism (angle ~30°) and place this prism in a glass trough with parallel sides filled with the solvent; this arrangement allows reversed spectra to be obtained with less concentrated (thus more transparent) solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immersion in the trough reduces the compensating effect of the solvent and makes abnormal dispersion easier to observe; useful when concentrated solutions are impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace solid prism with liquid-filled prism for spectroscope
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the ordinary glass prism of a spectroscope with a hollow prism filled with a concentrated solution (e.g., fuchsine) to observe reversed spectra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversed spectrum will be seen if the light is very strong and rays pass very close to the prism edge; with immersion in solvent trough, less light and looser geometry are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of dispersion on solution concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: The occurrence and character of abnormal dispersion depend on concentration: highly concentrated solutions show anomalous (reversed) dispersion; dilute solutions exhibit normal dispersion; intermediate concentrations can produce a single red line (compensation between abnormal and normal dispersion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust concentration to produce or remove the anomalous effect; note that for some substances (e.g., cyanine) anomalous dispersion appears only at high concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of angle of incidence and geometry on dispersion
rubrics_metrics.description: The observed dispersion varies with the angle of incidence and with prism geometry; the most favourable angle must be determined experimentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial-and-error is required to find optimal angles; quantitative examples given (e.g., with prism in air red deviates ~11°30′; when immersed violet scarcely deviates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing with solid particles and pressure can change spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Some bodies (potassium-permanganate, carmine) exhibit reversed spectra only when highly concentrated solutions are mixed with fine solid particles to form a pulp and the two glass plates are pressed strongly together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical state (suspension/pulp), presence of particles, and mechanical pressure can enable abnormal dispersion that is not present in clear solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation practice: light source and slit considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The dispersion observation is made by viewing through the liquid layer a narrow bright flame or an illuminated slit; strong light and rays passing close to prism edges improve visibility of reversed spectra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sufficiently strong, narrow source; when the prism is immersed in solvent, the required light intensity and proximity to the edge are reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive framework: apply metallic-reflection formulæ when reflection dominates
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies with surface‑colours behave like metals toward rays forming the surface colour (strong reflection) and like transparent media for other rays; in cases where rays are reflected in large proportion, the formulae of Cauchy for metallic reflection (and elliptic polarisation constants) should be used rather than ordinary transparent‑media dispersion formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect refractive indices that may be very large or even less than unity for certain colours; use elliptic polarisation data (Jamin, Quincke) to interpret anomalous behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for identifying abnormal dispersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Abnormal dispersion is indicated when the order of colours in the dispersion spectrum differs from that of the solar (ordinary) spectrum—for example, sequences like green, blue, red rather than the normal violet-to-red sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific substances give characteristic reordered sequences (e.g., cyanine: green, light blue, dark blue, dark interval, red, traces of orange); document ordering and compare with normal solar ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation effects between solvent and solute dispersions
rubrics_metrics.description: Anomalous dispersion due to a dissolved dye (solute) can be entirely compensated by the normal dispersion of the solvent at certain concentrations, yielding deviation without dispersion (e.g., a single red line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate concentration and immersion medium to observe compensation; immersing the prism in solvent can destroy solvent-induced deviation while leaving anomalous dispersion of solute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reporting of observed deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record numerical deviations (angles) observed under different conditions (e.g., deviation of red about 11°30′ in air; when immersed in alcohol violet scarcely deviated, red by 15', orange by 23').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise angular measurements and experimental conditions (concentration, medium, geometry) to allow reproducibility and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of scientific description and specimen preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality scientific work is characterised by thoroughness of research, clearness and accuracy of descriptions, detailed monographs with illustrations, and preservation of types/specimens (loss of types is a serious calamity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish complete descriptions with illustrations; safeguard type specimens against loss (museum practices, duplicates, distribution) to sustain long-term scientific value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing authenticity and reliability of field/telegraphic reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The authenticity of telegraphic or field intelligence should be judged by source credibility (e.g., caution of the reporter), corroborating dispatches, and documentary details like dates; cautious, reliable reporters increase confidence in received intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek corroboration, consider the reputation and known caution of the informant, and treat undated or single-source telegrams with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for phyto-geographic and natural-history interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical and phyto‑climatic studies should be based on careful investigation of climatic conditions and methodised data, with copious references; avoid over‑estimating the role of climate or invoking mysterious forces while neglecting consequences of historical possession, invasions, and natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise empirical exploration, thorough data compilation, and cautious, well-referenced interpretation rather than speculative or non‑empirical explanations.
